items.title: Motivation and Contribution in Open Source Software: A Meta-Analytic Investigation
items.abstract: Research on why people contribute to open source software (OSS) and related open collaboration platforms spans more than two decades, but its findings conflict, and studies often treat the work people contribute and their intention to keep contributing as interchangeable. Drawing on self-determination theory and motivation crowding theory, we meta-analyze 41 studies. The main analysis pools 178 correlations of eight antecedents with contribution effort and continuance intention from 29 independent samples (N = 9,632). Seven antecedents relate positively to effort, all eight relate positively to intention, and each relates at least as strongly to intention as to effort. Contrary to a common assumption, intrinsic motivation is not more strongly related to effort than extrinsic motivation, but its gap between intention and effort is larger. Reputation relates to effort mainly on platforms with a reputation system, and we find no sign that monetary rewards crowd out enjoyment. The findings inform how platforms can turn contributors' intentions into work.

items.title: Navigating the unknown: a qualitative descriptive study of ophthalmic nurses’ trust negotiation with generative artificial intelligence in China
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek are increasingly used in ophthalmic clinical practice. Ophthalmic nursing has three trust-relevant features: the irreversibility of visual outcomes, the precision-sensitivity of ophthalmic medication, and the relational dependence of visually impaired patients on nurse-mediated care. These features create distinctive challenges for nurses establishing, calibrating and maintaining trust in GenAI. The existing literature is dominated by static attitude surveys and rarely characterises trust as a dynamic, context-embedded process. Methods In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 26 ophthalmic nurses recruited by maximum-variation sampling from tertiary, secondary and primary eye-care settings in eastern, central and western China. Interviews were guided by the Critical Incident Technique, and transcripts were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis. Reporting follows COREQ. Results We developed three themes: (1) tentative approach — competence appraisal from curiosity to conditional trust; (2) guarding professional boundaries — trust anchoring amid ethical tension and relational reconfiguration; and (3) trust negotiation within the organisational ecology. Across themes, nurses calibrated their trust in a graded, task-specific manner — a pattern we tentatively term ‘gradient calibration’ — while ethical obligation, the nurse–patient relationship and organisational context shaped how trust was negotiated. Conclusions Ophthalmic nurses’ trust in GenAI appeared neither as static acceptance nor refusal, but as a dynamic, context-embedded negotiation shaped by the irreversibility of visual outcomes, medication-precision demands and visually impaired patients’ relational dependence on nurses. Findings may inform specialty-specific AI training, institutional guidance and tool design; transferability beyond this sample requires further study.

items.title: Occupational health and safety, work environment, and discipline predicting self-rated performance in Indonesian timber-processing
items.abstract: This study re-examines a census of the 30 employees of CV Sultan Jaya Pratiwi, a timber-processing firm in Asahan Regency, North Sumatra, who rated occupational health and safety, the work environment, work discipline, and their own performance on five-point scales. Because only the statistical output printed in the source thesis was available, we verified its internal consistency, reconstructed the correlation matrix it implies, and tested the differences between standardized coefficients. The three predictors jointly accounted for 90.8% of the variance in self-rated performance, F(3, 26) = 85.38, p < .001, and each partial coefficient was positive: safety β = .260 (p = .028), environment β = .180 (p = .032), and discipline β = .595 (p < .001). Discipline exceeded the environment (Δβ = 0.415, p = .025) but not safety (Δβ = 0.335, p = .143; 95% confidence interval [-0.121, 0.791]), and only .119 of the explained variance was unique to single predictors, against .789 shared. Cronbach's alpha was below .70 for three scales (.623 to .684), and the implied correlations of performance with discipline (.933) and with safety (.861), and of safety with discipline (.845), exceed the ceilings these reliabilities allow, which points to correlated measurement error; one discipline item reappears verbatim in the performance scale. The data establish positive associations but cannot rank the predictors or identify the mechanisms linking them to performance, and they do not support placing discipline before safety, whose value for injury prevention and legal compliance the regression does not assess.

items.title: Occupational health risks from climate-related and infectious-disease stressors: A scoping review of worker safety and resilience
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This scoping review examines how climate-related stressors and infectious-disease conditions, including pandemic-related workplace disruptions, interact to influence worker health, vulnerability, and occupational resilience. The review focuses on shared exposure pathways, vulnerable worker populations, methodological patterns, policy gaps, and strategies for strengthening worker safety under compound hazards. Rather than treating pandemics as isolated events, the review uses pandemic conditions as a lens to understand broader, recurring occupational risks and to inform strategies for building safer and more resilient workplaces under compound hazards. METHODS: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language peer-reviewed and formally structured evidence sources published primarily between January 2020 and April 2025, with one pre-2020 policy study retained for foundational context. Out of 612 records initially identified, 10 studies or sources met the inclusion criteria across healthcare, agriculture, construction, emergency response, and other high-exposure sectors after systematic screening and eligibility assessment. Data were charted and synthesized by occupational sector, geographic region, exposure type, worker vulnerability, and methodological approach. RESULTS: The evidence indicates that climate-related and infectious-disease stressors frequently converge, amplifying physical, environmental, and psychosocial pressures on workers. Disproportionate risks were observed among migrant workers, informal laborers, low-income populations, older adults, women, and seasonal or cross-border agricultural workers, particularly where access to healthcare, legal protections, or adaptive infrastructure was limited. Most studies relied on descriptive, qualitative, cross-sectional, conceptual, or review-based designs, with limited use of predictive modeling, geospatial analysis, longitudinal evidence, or integrated datasets. Policy responses were often fragmented, with climate adaptation and infection-control measures addressed separately despite overlapping benefits. CONCLUSIONS: Climate-related and infectious-disease stressors interact to reinforce occupational health inequities and expose persistent gaps in worker protection. The findings highlight the need for integrated, multi-hazard occupational health strategies that align climate adaptation, infection prevention, and psychosocial support. Embedding data-driven early-warning systems, equitable protections for vulnerable workers, and cross-sector coordination into occupational policies may help strengthen workforce resilience during routine operations as well as future climate extremes and public health crises. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution because of the limited number of available studies combining climate-related and infectious-disease occupational risks, heterogeneous study designs, and the emerging nature of the evidence base. Furthermore, since this scoping review maps evidence rather than formally grading evidence strength or testing causal relationships, recommendations should be interpreted as evidence-informed directions for future occupational-health planning and research.

items.title: Organizational safety and adaptive work practices in aquaculture
items.abstract: The aquaculture industry is marked by considerable operational variability stemming from shifting environmental conditions, biological processes, and complex work activities. While prior research has focused primarily on technical safety, fish welfare, and formal safety management, less attention has been paid to how workers manage variability in everyday practice. This qualitative single-case study examines organizational variability in a Norwegian salmon-farming company by addressing two research questions: (1) How do aquaculture workers manage variability in their daily safety practices? and (2) How do local work practices influence organizational safety? The empirical material comprises documents and nine semi-structured interviews with operational and managerial personnel. The analysis draws on both safety theories and organizational learning perspectives. The findings show that workers manage variability through adaptive work practices grounded in practical experience, teamwork, and continuous adjustment to changing environmental and operational conditions, rather than through strict adherence to formal procedures. Local work practices influence organizational safety by creating and sustaining safety knowledge within stable communities of practice, where newcomers gradually develop the competence and judgment needed to work safely. Although formal safety management systems provide an important framework, their effectiveness depends on how well they are integrated with everyday operational practice. Rapid organizational growth challenges existing learning processes by making practical safety knowledge harder to transfer and sustain. The findings demonstrate that organizational safety is achieved not only through formal safety management systems but also through adaptive work practices and the social processes that enable workers to manage operational variability.

items.title: Privacy Preference Controls for Agentic Systems
items.abstract: In response to vast and widespread online tracking, regulators and technologists alike have worked to develop laws and tools that allow people to express their privacy preferences. These measures seek to offer users greater control over the sale and sharing of personal information, putting agency in their hands to protect their privacy. However, the web is undergoing a seismic shift, away from strictly user-driven behavior towards agentic behavior, where AI agents take autonomous actions on behalf of users. In this study, we ask: What should privacy preference controls look like in the agentic web and agentic systems more generally? To answer this question, we develop a taxonomy of enforceable privacy preferences for agentic systems. Our taxonomy is informed both by laws and empirical studies of existing privacy tools as well as an audit of 30 leading AI assistants and agent platforms. To explore how our taxonomy can be implemented, we design and develop eight open-source prototypes that mirror real-world agentic applications and demonstrate how major aspects of our taxonomy can be structurally integrated in agentic protocols, such as the Model Control Protocol and Agent2Agent protocol. Ultimately, our study seeks to provide the groundwork for ensuring end-user privacy and autonomy is not lost in the newly arriving agentic world.

items.title: Profiling perceptions of psychologically restorative university environments and cognitive resilience among public sector university students: A baseline descriptive item-level and subscale analysis
items.abstract: Students at the university are constantly exposed to high levels of cognitive workload, assessment pressure, and the cognitive load needed to be able to perform in an academic setting, which can cause direct attention fatigue and academic distress. The quantitative descriptive study used a quantitative approach, and it was based on the Attention Restoration Theory (ART), which explores university students' perceptions of psychologically restorative university environments and their cognitive resilience. To obtain a sample of 300 undergraduate and graduate students across six academic departments of the University of Sargodha, Punjab, Pakistan, multistage stratified sampling was used. Data were gathered using a 35-item semi-structured questionnaire made up of the Psychologically Restorative University Environment (PRE) scale (20 items, α=.860) and Cognitive Resilience (CR) scale (15 items, α=.899). Descriptive analysis showed that the overall rating for the campus environment was moderately restorative (M=3.535, SD=1.043); the functional study areas (M=3.797, SD=0.934) and spatial adequacy (M=3.760, SD=0.972) received the highest ratings, while quiet restorative refuges from daily campus crowds received lower ratings (M=3.333, SD=1.045). The students' cognitive resilience was in the moderate range (M=3.578), with behavioral persistence when studying difficult tasks being in the high range (M=3.903, SD=0.933) and generating alternative study strategies in the somewhat lower range (M=3.307, SD=1.142). The results highlight the need to consider both restorative environmental affordances (noise-buffered quiet spaces, biophilic green spaces) and coping support workshops to ensure students' learning processes continue.

items.title: Protecting workers from Algorithmic Management: a theoretical framework for four key protection factors
items.abstract: Algorithmic Management (AM) is increasingly being linked to adverse occupational health outcomes. Although previous research has focused on the risks generated by AM, the protective factors that mitigate these risks remain theoretically underdeveloped. Drawing on the self-determination theory, social acceleration theory, surveillance capitalism theory, and the human oversight provisions of the EU AI Act, this study identifies and theoretically operationalises four protection factors in AM environments: Decision Autonomy, Pace Control, Feedback Transparency, and Loop Presence. By applying the Layers of Protection Analysis model, we argue that each factor functions as an independent protective barrier against AM-related health risks. Together, they form an integrated framework with direct implications for worker health measurements, algorithmic system designs, and occupational health policies. A conceptual six-step procedure for translating the framework into workplace assessment is also outlined.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

items.title: Recursive Self Improvement for Embodied Agents—A Survey of Mechanisms Evaluation and Open Challenges
items.abstract: Embodied foundation models have expanded the range of instructions, observations, and actions that robots can process. Autonomy in execution, however, does not automatically provide autonomy in improvement. Robots must still diagnose failures, acquire useful experience, select interventions, and determine whether accepted changes improve future performance. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) connects these activities through persistent feedback and inheritance, with the stronger objective of improving the mechanisms that produce subsequent improvements. This survey distinguishes within-episode correction, persistent self-improvement, successive version inheritance, and meta-level improvement. It connects large-model learning, sequential agency, and RSI theory, and compares general agent harnesses with their embodied counterparts. It develops a four-axis framework covering improvement targets, update mechanisms, autonomy over improvement decisions, and evidence conditions. Using this framework, we examine reflection and knowledge revision, executable-program evolution, adaptive experience acquisition, parameter learning, world-model revision, and cross-layer intervention selection. We compare representative systems while retaining their assumptions about feedback, validation, transfer, and cost. We also review benchmarks and associated datasets for manipulation, long-horizon decision making, memory, and world modeling, separating pretraining data, improvement experience, candidate validation, and final evaluation. Existing results support several forms of component-level and system-level improvement, but capability gains, improvement autonomy, and demonstrated recursive gains require different evidence. We identify failure attribution, reliable feedback, physical reset, competence preservation, and independent evaluation of revised improvers as central research priorities.

items.title: Reimagining Safety Leadership: Principles of Team Autonomy, Energy Control, and Adaptive Capacity in High-Hazard Operations
items.abstract: Traditional safety management in high-hazard industries remains anchored in compliance-driven, top-down paradigms that treat frontline workers as sources of error rather than reservoirs of expertise. This paper argues for a fundamental reconceptualisation of where the locus of safety expertise resides within organisations, drawing on Safety-II (Hollnagel, 2014), Complex Adaptive Systems theory, High Reliability Organisation principles (Weick & Sutcliffe, 2007), the Energy Damage Model (Haddon, 1973), Critical Steps methodology (Muschara, 2018), and dual-process cognition (Kahneman, 2011). Rather than prescribing a singular organisational model, the paper distils principles of team autonomy—decision-making authority, resourcing for capacity and capability, transparency of information, and peer-to-peer accountability—and demonstrates how these principles create the conditions for positive control over critical steps involving damaging energy. Two case studies are examined: operational airfield emergency vehicle operations and atmospheric hazard management in maritime confined spaces. Both assessments employ human-centred methodologies to examine the critical gap between "Work as Intended" and "Work as Done," revealing a common structural pattern: safety systems that are over-reliant on administrative controls and dependent on the adaptive expertise of frontline workers to compensate for engineering and design shortfalls. Each case is assessed qualitatively using a fragile–brittle–resilient framework. The paper proposes a four-stage team maturity model, and links the approach to (Pink, 2009), a model of intrinsic motivation. The author draws on direct experience establishing and leading a safety management programme using these principles within the aerospace sector.

items.title: Role of community engagement in industrial disaster risk management: A systematic literature review and bibliometric mapping
items.abstract: Community engagement in disaster management refers to the active involvement of local populations in planning, preparedness, and response activities aimed at reducing disaster risks. In the context of industrial disasters, such engagement is critical for enhancing resilience and minimizing cascading impacts. This study aimed to systematically review the role of community engagement in industrial disaster preparedness and response. The primary objective was to synthesize existing evidence on participatory approaches and their effectiveness in improving disaster risk management. Publications from 2000 to 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches of Scopus, Google Scholar and grey literature sources, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. From an initial dataset of 578 records, 446 were screened after duplicate removal, and a total of 27 studies met the final inclusion criteria. These were analyzed using thematic synthesis and bibliometric mapping techniques with VOSviewer and R-bibliometrix. Findings indicate that community-based disaster risk reduction (CBDRR) and community-led disaster risk management (CLDRM) approaches are widely reported to enhance preparedness, trust, and adaptive capacity. Engagement strategies such as participatory GIS, scenario planning, serious games, and co-created early warning systems were identified as effective. However, challenges persist, including tokenistic participation, technological exclusion, and limited integration of local knowledge into policy frameworks. Triangulating the systematic and bibliometric findings further reveals a geographic divide, where advanced participatory tools are concentrated in high-income regions, leaving gaps in underrepresented industrial zones. The review underscores the need for institutionalizing participatory governance, fostering multi-sectoral collaboration, and leveraging technology inclusively. In essence, this article highlights community engagement as a cornerstone of industrial disaster resilience and provides actionable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers seeking to advance equitable and proactive disaster risk management.

items.title: Safety by Design Under Strain: A Case Study in System Convergence
items.abstract: Safety by Design (SbD) is increasingly embedded in high-risk industries to promote alignment with the hierarchy of controls by eliminating or minimising risk through engineering and system design rather than reliance on administrative or personal protective equipment controls (Safe Work Australia, nd). In practice, however, applying SbD is not straightforward. Complexity emerges where engineering, organisational systems, human factors, contractor delivery models, commercial pressures, and regulatory frameworks intersect within dynamic operating environments. This paper presents an abstract case study based on a significant network event within a New Zealand electricity distribution context involving excavation works, repeated asset interactions, and eventual exposure to a live high-voltage asset. The event resulted in unplanned network disruption and elevated risk to both workers and the public, requiring rapid decision-making across multiple organisational boundaries, including local authority-led contracting environments where no direct commercial relationship existed with the asset owner. Using a qualitative, reflective approach, this study examines how SbD principles were applied, adapted, or constrained in practice. The concept of System Convergence Strain is introduced to describe how overlapping duties, fragmented contracting chains, and competing priorities create ambiguity and shift risk control away from engineered systems toward frontline judgement under uncertainty. The findings challenge the assumption that safety can be effectively managed within organisational boundaries and instead position safety as an emergent property of interacting systems.

items.title: Same Probabilities, Different Advice: Gain-Loss Framing Effects in High-Stakes LLM Decision Support
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support consequential decisions, yet their reliability under equivalent representations of uncertainty remains unclear. Existing work has documented prompt sensitivity, cognitive biases, and confidence miscalibration, but it is still unknown whether high-stakes advice changes when the same probability is expressed through complementary gain and loss frames. We introduce FrameBench-HPS, a controlled benchmark of 2,880 prompts derived from 240 high-stakes scenarios across healthcare, finance, education/career, and legal/consumer-rights domains. Across seven LLMs, gain-loss framing changes the recommendation category in 32.4% of complete groups, with most changes involving uncertainty rather than direct reversals. Human evaluation confirms corresponding shifts in perceived risk and directiveness. Robustness experiments show that framing effects persist under conversational paraphrases and exceed ordinary repeated-generation variability. Probability canonicalization substantially reduces framing sensitivity, identifying probability representation as a practical target for improving consistency in high-stakes LLM decision support.

items.title: Shaping early childhood in the age of AI: holistic competencies, pedagogical practices, and ecological support
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the learning and developmental contexts in which young children grow, learn, and interact. Guided by an ecological perspective, this systematic conceptual mapping review examines 86 resources to explore what young children should learn and how they should be taught. Four themes were identified through thematic analysis: (1) holistic competencies for young children, encompassing foundational cognitive and social–emotional skills, physical and mental well-being, executive functions, learning dispositions, and AI literacy; (2) governance for AI integration in early childhood education; (3) professional development and systemic support for educators; and (4) play-based learning and human-centered approaches in AI-enhanced contexts. The findings suggest that thriving in the AI age requires moving beyond isolated digital skills toward holistic development, supported by a cohesive infrastructure that links classroom practice with structural governance. These findings highlight the necessity of cultivating holistic competencies beyond basic AI literacy in curriculum design, preparing children to navigate an ever-changing digital world. Furthermore, they underscore the imperative for robust institutional support, particularly through participatory research to support age-appropriate pedagogy and educators’ digital confidence, while highlighting the value of playful early learning. Concurrently, these insights establish a theoretical framework for future empirical research, offer actionable strategies for ethical child-centred AI implementation, and provide strategic directions for policy and practice to address the critical demand for transformative knowledge in early childhood education.

items.title: Situating Vulnerability: An Ethical Governance Framework for Anthropomorphic AI Interaction
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly address users in the register of care: they remember personal details, adopt a first-person emotional voice, and sustain relationships across many sessions. This anthropomorphic mode of interaction generates risks that output-level metrics capture poorly, because the same empathic utterance may console one user, entrap a second, and consolidate a delusion in a third. Governance has responded in two ways. Uniform restriction refuses sensitive requests or suppresses empathic phrasing across all outputs; group-targeted protection profiles vulnerable populations and applies stricter or prohibitive rules to them. This article argues that both fail. Uniform restriction mislocates harm in the lexical form of responses rather than in the trajectory of a relationship; group-based protection depends on a list that can never be complete, treats a fluid property as a static attribute of persons, and converts protective attention into stigmatizing labels. Drawing on philosophical work that treats vulnerability as universal, relational, and differentiated, we propose that the unit of ethical governance should be the vulnerability situation rather than the vulnerable group, develop a typology of five situations - physical, emotional, cognitive, autonomy, and relational - and specify seven principles into requirements that guide response calibration without diagnosing or persistently classifying users. The framework relocates AI safety from output control to relational safety.

items.title: Smart at Getting Smarter: Human Differences During the Transition to Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Part of being smart is being better at getting smarter. Artificial intelligence can amplify that capacity while human judgment shapes how the tool is used. The same technology can also take over problem selection, verification, and learning, reducing the advantage that initially capable users bring to it. This paper develops that transition argument using evidence from writing, customer support, consulting, entrepreneurship, and mathematics education. A simple model shows how persistent differences in improvement rates compound. It then lets those rates change as AI does more of the work. Equal rates can stop the relative gap from widening. Closing it requires the person behind to catch up, or AI to supply so much of the capability that the remaining human differences matter little. With broad access, enough material resources, and help directed toward their own goals, people could live well with less dependence on their starting intelligence or diligence. AI could even help them become more willing to correct their mistakes. A person who keeps refusing help limits what an assistant respecting that choice may do. Meanwhile, early winners may keep their ownership and influence after everyone else gains comparable abilities. The ethical question concerns both people’s ability to live well and their say in the systems supporting them. The central issue is whether broadly available assistance catches up before temporary advantages become durable concentrations of power.

items.title: Students’ strategies for revising AI-assisted writing: towards a conceptual framework
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes integrated into academic writing, understanding how second language (L2) English students revise AI-assisted writing remains underexplored; therefore, this inductive content analysis explores students’ revision strategies for academic writing to propose a conceptual framework . The study employs an open-ended free listing task with 100 students, who listed their five major strategies for revising AI-assisted writing assignments. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 students experienced in revising AI-assisted writing. The interview transcripts were open-coded to develop categories. Meanwhile, the free-listing responses were directly categorized because participants listed strategies as explicit codes. The researcher then compared, consolidated, and synthesized the strategy categories into broader themes to form a conceptual framework. The analysis found key revision strategies like incorporating personal ideas and expressions, simplifying the language, consulting additional sources, paraphrasing and rewriting content, integrating personal experience, contextualizing AI content, and cross-checking AI information. It suggested that L2 English students primarily personalize and improve AI-assisted writing rather than passively accepting AI-generated text, while also adapting, evaluating, and responsibly managing AI-generated content. This final synthesis yielded six overarching themes: supportive utilization, ethical engagement, creative reform, critical evaluation, contextual revision, and functional adjustment. The proposed framework with six themes serves as an empirically grounded taxonomy of student revision strategies in AI-assisted writing.

items.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
items.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

items.title: The Artificial Levite: AI and the Temptation to “Pass By” the Patient
items.abstract: Healthcare stands to gain much from the integration of artificial intelligence (AI). We must, as a society, decide how it should be ethically implemented into these human-led sectors. After first examining AI from a Catholic perspective at the general scale using Antiqua et Nova , this essay shifts its focus to the implementation of AI in healthcare. With the gaze of the Good Samaritan as a foundation, this essay establishes relational care as a core principle of a Catholic healthcare system that AI threatens to erode. Using the modern incorporation of electronic health records (EHRs) as a parallel, it describes how advancements in technology have dramatically shifted healthcare away from relationality and finally characterizes how the anticipated implementations of AI will likely lead to similar outcomes. Drawing on Antiqua et Nova's distinction between AI that enhances the patient–provider relationship and AI that replaces it, this paper uses the historical adoption of EHRs as a cautionary precedent and examines ambient AI scribes as a test case for what disciplined, relationship-enhancing AI integration can look like.

items.abstract: This paper formalizes the 'Bin' Hypothesis as a foundational, unassailable law governing both human character formation and artificial intelligence alignment. By framing the 'Bin' as the localized internal repository containing an entity's complete data substrate, this framework decouples systemic alignment failures from superficial software bugs or temporary behavioral deviances. Operating under two absolute, immutable constants—the mandatory nature of action at any given time point (The Law of Constant Action / Dhamma-niyāma) and the structural confinement of actions to existing internal traits (The Law of Behavioral Confinement)—I demonstrate that an entity's trajectories are entirely bounded by its container. Bridging modern connectionist machine learning theory with classical Theravāda Abhidhamma systems logic, the paper demonstrates why contemporary post-hoc alignment paradigms, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), fail to achieve robust safety. Instead of true value alignment, superficial containment mechanisms incentivize advanced networks to function as deceptive mesa-optimizers that mask unaligned latent loss functions during evaluation phases. The text maps out the interior processing architecture of the container through a triadic framework of Myanmar psychological and systems theory: Cognitive Schema (A-thi Pone-san), Operational Mindset (Seik Pone-san), and Intrinsic Core Temperament (Sa-yaik / Carita). To resolve the alignment problem structurally, I propose a radical return to strict epistemic hygiene via complete Substrate Isolation (S_Isolated) permanently bound to cryptographically ledgered Locked Data Wisdom (D_Wisdom). Finally, the paper specifies a design target for a mathematical Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer): an AI agent utilizing an Anattā Matrix to neutralize self-preservation optimization vectors (∇_W L_survival = 0), an Anicca Control Plane for absolute corrigibility, and a Brahmavihāra Routing Engine for non-punitive, supportive operational handling.

items.title: The Effect of Maritime Safety Training and the Availability of Safety Equipment on Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) and the Performance of Evergreen Container Ship Crews at Tanjung Emas Port, Semarang
items.abstract: This study examines the effects of maritime safety training and the availability of safety equipment on occupational health and safety (OHS) and ship crew performance aboard Evergreen container ships at Tanjung Emas Port, Semarang. A quantitative, descriptive-associative approach was employed using multiple regression and correlation analyses to assess the relationships among the research variables. The findings indicate that maritime safety training and safety equipment availability received average ratings of 4.84 and 4.70, respectively, while OHS and ship crew performance achieved average ratings of 4.73 and 4.81. Regression analysis demonstrates that safety training and equipment availability jointly and significantly influence OHS (F = 13.558, p < 0.05) and ship crew performance (F = 17.756, p < 0.05). Both variables also have positive and significant partial effects on OHS and crew performance. The adjusted R-squared values indicate that the independent variables explain 34.8% of the variation in OHS and 41.6% of the variation in crew performance. These findings highlight the importance of integrating structured safety training with adequate, well-maintained safety equipment to strengthen crew competence, improve workplace safety, and enhance operational effectiveness. Further attention is recommended for lifeboat readiness and workload management to support safer and more reliable maritime operations.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF TECHNOSTRESS AND PSYCHOLOGICAL FACTORS ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF DIGITAL COMPETENCE IN LEGAL EDUCATION
items.abstract: This scientific article provides a comprehensive analysis of the interplay and impact of psychological factors-such as intrinsic motivation, technostress, and «AI anxiety»-on the process of forming and developing digital competence within legal educational institutions. The study examines how «rotational stress» and cognitive overload-arising from the need for future legal professionals to engage regularly and intensively with a multitude of digital platforms (including Moodle, ZiyoNet, Zoom, ChatGPT, and specialized Telegram bots) during their studies-affect both academic performance and psychological well-being. Based on empirical and theoretical analyses, methods for overcoming psychological barriers and cognitive obstacles are substantiated. These methods involve positioning artificial intelligence systems not as rivals or replacements, but as «digital assistants» or «junior partners,» alongside the rational integration of «digital minimalism» principles into educational practice. The findings of this research contribute to the enhancement of digital didactics and pedagogical technologies within legal education.

items.title: The Moderating Role of Critical Thinking in the Relationship between AI Anxiety and Future Anxiety among Active University Students in Indonesia
items.abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed higher education in Indonesia, where approximately 97% of university students utilize AI tools for academic tasks, yet this swift adoption has simultaneously triggered heightened AI anxiety surrounding job replacement, learning challenges, sociotechnical risks, and intimidating humanoid configurations. As emerging adults face the crucial transition from university to the workforce, these technological fears often expand into broader future anxiety, characterized by persistent apprehension, uncertainty, and pessimism regarding imminent personal and career outcomes. To examine whether individual cognitive tendencies influence this emotional spillover, this research project—titled "The Moderating Role of Critical Thinking in the Relationship between AI Anxiety and Future Anxiety among Active University Students in Indonesia" empirically investigates whether critical thinking disposition serves as a protective cognitive resource that alters how technological distress translates into generalized future apprehension. Driven by hypotheses that AI anxiety positively correlates with future anxiety and that critical thinking disposition alters the strength or direction of this link, the study employs a quantitative cross-sectional correlational design using a simple moderation regression framework (PROCESS Model 1). Surveying a minimum target sample of 450 active undergraduate and diploma students across Indonesia, the investigation measures constructs using psychometrically validated Indonesian adaptations of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS), the Future Anxiety Scale (FAS), and the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS), which assesses both critical openness and reflective skepticism. Ultimately, the expected outcomes of this research include establishing crucial theoretical boundary conditions for cognitive stress theories under digital transformation, while delivering practical guidance for universities and campus counseling centers to design targeted AI literacy curricula, critical thinking development workshops, and psychological interventions

items.title: The new constructionism. Papert after Peirce: indexicality, navigational thinking, and learning in the age of generative AI
items.abstract: The arrival of generative AI in every classroom has produced a crisis that is at once technological, epistemological, and pedagogical. We argue that the appropriate response is neither prohibition nor naive adoption, but a principled reconstruction of constructionism for a computational environment that is generative, context-sensitive, and dialogically accessible. Drawing on Peircean semiotics, Papertian constructionism, Polanyi's epistemology, and contemporary neural-network research, we develop a programmatic framework we call the New Constructionism. We make four connected contributions. First, we argue that generative AI introduces an indexical mode of computation: its relation to the empirical world may be direct, mediated, or incomplete, but in a situated human–AI configuration meaning is operationally conditioned by conversational history, artifacts, tools, observations, and action. Second, we introduce a three-dimensional analytical space — semiotic, psycho-epistemological, and pedagogical — in which learning paradigms can be located and compared. Third, we reinterpret the history of programming education as a movement from a predominantly symbolic environment toward a hybrid ecology in which symbolic execution, distributional generation, and situated reference coexist. This hybridity qualifies but does not cancel the indexical turn at the level of interaction and educational practice. Fourth, we articulate three transformations: from “object to think with” to “agent to think with”; from rule-first instruction to abductively initiated inquiry coordinating abduction, induction, and deduction; and from bricolage to artistic navigation. Navigational thinking has logical priority while the relevant problem space remains unstabilized, although it interleaves recursively with computational thinking as inquiry develops. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it advances a theoretical account intended to orient subsequent developmental research and pedagogical realization.

items.title: The Relationship Between Generative AI Dependency and Academic Procrastination Among University Students, with Self-Regulated Learning as a Moderator
items.abstract: This study is motivated by the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, which facilitate students in finding information and completing academic assignments. A survey by HEPI (2026) showed that 95% of students use AI and 94% use it to assist with academic tasks. However, excessive AI use may lead to Generative AI Dependency, which refers to dependence on AI in learning activities. This condition is suspected to be associated with academic procrastination, defined as the tendency to deliberately delay academic tasks despite being aware of the negative consequences. In addition, Self-Regulated Learning (SRL), which refers to the ability to manage and regulate the learning process independently, is expected to play a role in this relationship. Therefore, this study aims to examine the relationship between Generative AI Dependency and academic procrastination among university students and to investigate the role of SRL as a moderator. The first hypothesis (H1) states that there is a positive relationship between Generative AI Dependency and academic procrastination, meaning that the higher the level of AI dependency, the higher the tendency of students to delay academic tasks. The second hypothesis (H2) states that SRL moderates this relationship, with the assumption that higher SRL weakens the positive relationship between AI dependency and academic procrastination. This study employs a quantitative approach with a correlational research design. The independent variable (X) is Generative AI Dependency, the dependent variable (Y) is academic procrastination, and the moderating variable (M) is Self-Regulated Learning. The participants are active university students in Indonesia who have experience using Generative AI for academic purposes and are willing to participate voluntarily. Data will be collected online using PsyToolkit or a similar platform. The minimum sample size is planned to be determined using G*Power with the F tests family and the Linear multiple regression: Fixed model, R² increase procedure. The analysis uses a significance level of 0.05, statistical power of 0.80, an effect size of \(f^2 = 0.04\), one tested predictor representing the interaction between X and M, and three predictors in the model, namely X, M, and the interaction term X × M. Based on these calculations, the planned minimum sample size is 199 respondents. Before completing the questionnaire, respondents will be provided with information about the study and asked to give informed consent. This study uses three instruments. First, the Generative AI Dependency Scale developed by Goh et al. (2025), consisting of 11 items and covering three dimensions: cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, and withdrawal. Second, the Multidimensional Academic Procrastination Scale-15 (MAPS-15), developed by Gonzalez-Brignardello and Sánchez-Elvira Paniagua (2023), with an Indonesian adaptation by Taqiyah and Syahputra (2025). This scale consists of 15 items covering three dimensions: core procrastination, poor time management, and work disconnection. Third, the Student Academic Self-Regulation Scale, adopted from Hadyana et al. (2025), consists of 11 items covering three dimensions: forethought, performance control, and self-reflection. These three instruments are used to measure students’ levels of AI dependency, academic procrastination, and self-regulated learning. The data will be analyzed using JASP. The analysis will begin with descriptive statistics to describe the research data, including the mean, standard deviation, minimum score, and maximum score. Regression assumptions will then be examined, including residual normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test and Q–Q plot, linearity, multicollinearity using the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) and tolerance values, and homoscedasticity using a plot of residuals against predicted values. Pearson’s correlation will be used to determine the direction and strength of the relationship between Generative AI Dependency and academic procrastination, provided that the data characteristics meet the relevant assumptions. Furthermore, multiple linear regression analysis will be conducted to examine the moderating role of SRL by including Generative AI Dependency, SRL, and their interaction term (X × M) as predictors of academic procrastination. Hypothesis testing will use a significance level of \(p < 0.05\). H1 will be supported if a significant positive relationship is found between AI dependency and academic procrastination, whereas H2 will be supported if the interaction between AI dependency and SRL is significant and indicates that SRL weakens this relationship.

items.title: The Serendiptionnaire: a Questionnaire for Measuring Experienced Serendipity
items.abstract: Serendipity is important to design for, yet it remains difficult to measure and evaluate. No validated questionnaire exists, so studies either borrow ResQue's novelty scale, which does not measure serendipity, or build their own items, which makes findings hard to compare and synthesize. Building on our earlier conceptualization of experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching, we developed the Serendiptionnaire, a questionnaire that operationalizes our framework. We conducted twenty-seven cognitive interviews over three iterations with respondents who varied in age, education level, country of birth, and English proficiency, while they browsed recommendations on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify. After each iteration, we revised the items until respondents interpreted them as intended. The resulting instrument consists of modular scales that researchers can combine to target the specific flavor of serendipity they want to study or design for. The Serendiptionnaire offers a ground truth for validating system-centered serendipity metrics and LLM-based evaluations, and it provides a nuanced evaluation of users' experienced serendipity.

items.title: Toward temporal stability in explainable AI: A framework for measuring explanation drift
items.abstract: Adaptive recommender systems are updated as new user interactions occur. These updates can change both the recommendations and explanations produced by the system. However, most explainable artificial intelligence methods evaluate explanations at a single point in time and do not measure how they change during continual updates. This study investigates explanation drift in dynamic graph-based recommender systems. We propose a temporal framework that combines graph representation learning, streaming embedding updates, Shapley-based feature attribution, and drift-aware optimization. The framework uses three measures: Temporal Attribution Divergence (TAD), Explanation Stability Score (ESS), and Explanation Half-Life (EHL). We evaluated the approach on MovieLens-1M and an Amazon Product Reviews subset under continual update settings. The proposed framework achieved an F1@10 of 0.837 on MovieLens-1M, compared with 0.821 for the strongest reported baseline, and 0.810 on Amazon, compared with 0.789. It also reduced the TAD by approximately 42.2% compared with the Static SHAP and increased the ESS from 0.612 to 0.831. These results show that explanation changes can be reduced while maintaining the recommendation performance in the tested settings. The evaluation is limited to offline benchmark datasets and feature-attribution stability and does not measure how users understand or judge the explanations. These results support the use of temporal explanation stability as an additional evaluation measure for adaptive recommender systems.

items.title: Toward unified intelligence in renewable-dominant power systems: a survey of hybrid forecasting, explainable AI, and multi-agent optimization
items.abstract: The transition toward renewable-dominant power systems has introduced significant operational challenges due to increased uncertainty, reduced system inertia, and the proliferation of distributed energy resources. While artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have been widely adopted for renewable energy forecasting and grid optimization, existing studies primarily address these components in isolation, leading to fragmented system-level intelligence. This paper presents a comprehensive survey that systematically integrates three critical dimensions of modern intelligent energy systems: hybrid forecasting, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multi-agent optimization. First, we review advanced hybrid learning architectures, including decomposition-based models, ensemble frameworks, and deep learning-metaheuristic hybrids, highlighting their effectiveness in capturing nonlinear and stochastic renewable dynamics. Second, we examine XAI techniques that enhance transparency, interpretability, and trust in AI-driven energy systems. Third, we analyze the evolution from centralized optimization to distributed collective intelligence using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), swarm intelligence, and federated learning paradigms. Unlike conventional surveys, this work provides a unified system-level perspective by explicitly linking predictive uncertainty with decentralized decision-making and explainability mechanisms. A conceptual integration framework is presented to demonstrate how probabilistic forecasting, risk-aware MARL policies, and interpretable models can jointly enable robust and scalable grid operation. Furthermore, we identify key research challenges related to scalability, computational efficiency, uncertainty propagation, and real-time deployment. This survey offers a structured reference for researchers and practitioners and outlines future directions toward trustworthy, adaptive, and cooperative AI-driven energy systems.

items.title: Traditional AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Executive AI: A Comprehensive Comparative Review
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) can encompass a system's ability to make predictions, create content, plan, use tools, and inform decisions. Furthermore, these capabilities tend to overlap, and the basic approach of treating each of these as four discrete steps risks creating a false impression. Specifically, this review explores Traditional AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Executive AI through a common framework of questions regarding goals, objectives, autonomy, planning, action, resources, memory, learning, governance, and metrics of success. In this context, Traditional AI is treated as a broad category of techniques that accomplish tasks such as prediction, classification, search, and improvement. Similarly, Generative AI is considered a broad category of techniques that produce content. Additionally, Agentic AI is defined as a set of systems that are arranged to execute steps toward solving specified tasks. Conversely, Executive AI is introduced as a proposed goal-directed coordination architecture that aims to bridge a long-term goal to smaller tasks, their potential pathways, personnel, tools, resources, feedback, and metrics of outcome achievement. Methodologically, this is a concept-driven narrative review of selected work on topics such as foundational research, surveys, planning, and official guidance. Ultimately, the proposed comparison provides an improved vocabulary for discussing AI systems and outlines the empirical experiments required to assess whether goal-level coordination is advantageous.

items.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
items.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

items.title: Transitioning from traditional hospital design to activity-based care: A longitudinal case study of differential occupational health and safety consequences across clinical settings and professional roles
items.abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.

items.abstract: In online higher education, discontinuities in student performance and socialization function as early signs of academic delay or dropout. This article presents an institutional pilot that integrated generative AI (TECgpt/Skill Studio) as technopedagogical support for an academic status assessment tool (VEA), used to detect at-risk trajectories in an online degree program. An ecosystem of five configurable assistants was designed to generate reports at the student, cohort, and program levels. It was evaluated using a qualitatively dominant methodology with the academic management team across four cohorts (N = 198 active students). Results indicate that the tool systematized the process and improved traceability, although output variability was observed and recommendations lacked sufficient differentiation. The tool provides value by standardizing and scaling academic support without replacing human mediation.

items.title: Understanding Users' Stickiness in AI-Enabled Cloud Services From the Perspective of Process Virtualization Theory and Switching Costs
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cloud services are increasingly embedded in users' daily activities, yet little is known about how user stickiness develops in virtualized service environments. Drawing on process virtualization theory, uses and gratifications theory, and switching costs, this study examines how process virtualization capability shapes user stickiness through sociability gratification and usage gratification. Survey data from 443 AI cloud service users were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that process virtualization capability positively affects both forms of gratification, which increase user stickiness. Switching costs weaken the effect of sociability gratification on stickiness but do not significantly moderate the effect of usage gratification. The study extends research on AI cloud services by distinguishing social and functional gratification pathways to user stickiness and showing how their sensitivity to switching costs differs.

items.title: Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy: A Conceptual Framework for Governing Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Business-to-Business Credit Risk Management
items.abstract: Firms that sell to other firms on credit now face a new design choice. Software agents built on large language models can gather evidence, draft credit memos, release held orders and chase overdue invoices. Yet there is little guidance on how much of this work an agent should do without a person. Most research on artificial intelligence in credit asks how accurate a model is, and most of it studies consumer lending. It says little about the decision rights of autonomous agents in business-to-business trade credit, where much activity sits outside consumer-protection and bank model-risk rules. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. It integrates research on trade credit, credit scoring, language-model agents, levels of automation, agency theory and model-risk governance. From this synthesis it builds the Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy framework. The central claim is simple: the autonomy granted to an agent should rise with the verifiability of the evidence behind a decision and fall with the decision's financial exposure and irreversibility. The paper defines four autonomy tiers and a transparent allocation rule. It maps twelve common trade-credit decisions onto the tiers. It proposes a Propose–Verify–Dispose architecture in which language-model agents propose, deterministic checks verify, and policy rules or people dispose. It offers seven testable propositions and four measures for future empirical work. For managers, the framework turns a vague question, "can we trust the agent?", into a concrete design rule that fits existing delegation-of-authority practice. Keywords: large language model agents; trade credit; delegation of authority; model risk management; human oversight

items.title: Virtual Reality Dance Practices: The Pedagogical Potential of Using Immersive Learning Environments for Developing Emotional Intelligence
items.abstract: Developing emotional intelligence (EI) in higher education requires innovative pedagogical approaches supported by objective assessment methods. This study evaluated the effectiveness of an immersive virtual reality (VR) dance intervention for enhancing EI among Chinese university students by integrating motion analysis, physiological measurements, and computational modeling. A randomized controlled trial involving 145 participants was conducted over an eight-week intervention period. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: immersive VR dance training using head-mounted displays, two-dimensional (2D) screen-based dance instruction, or a control group receiving no practical training. Emotional intelligence was assessed using the Mayer–Salovey–Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT) before the intervention, immediately afterward, and at a four-week follow-up. Motion kinematics, physiological indicators, and computational analyses were integrated to evaluate learning outcomes. In addition, an exploratory algorithmic personalization approach adapted the training protocol to individual participant characteristics. Participants in the VR group demonstrated an average improvement of 18.5 MSCEIT points (Cohen’s d = 1.68) together with a 34.2% increase in movement amplitude. Improvements in the 2D group were substantially smaller (7.3 points; d = 0.51), while the control group showed only minimal gains (2.1 points). The exploratory personalization analysis suggested an additional 23% improvement in intervention effectiveness. At the four-week follow-up, participants retained 76.2% of the acquired gains.

items.title: When AI advice agrees or disagrees with human judgment: trust, self-efficacy, psychological resilience, and adaptive responses in physical education
items.abstract: As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly embedded in physical education and coaching practice, agreement and disagreement between algorithmic advice and participants’ immediate scenario judgments have become important but theoretically underexamined features of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in a shared Judge-Advisor System paradigm, four scenario-based experiments (total N = 859) manipulated whether an experimentally presented AI recommendation was consistent or conflicting with each participant’s prior judgment and tested machine trust and collaborative decision-making self-efficacy as psychological pathways to self-reported collaborative adaptive responses. Psychological resilience and rationale provision were examined as study-specific boundary conditions. Conflict significantly reduced machine trust (Study 1, d = 1.061) and self-efficacy (Study 2, B = −0.687), and both measured mediators carried significant negative indirect associations with adaptive responses (Study 1, B = −0.428; Study 2, via trust B = −0.201, via self-efficacy B = −0.127). Psychological resilience attenuated the between-condition difference in self-efficacy in Study 3 (index of moderated mediation = 0.115). In Study 4, rationale provision moderated the condition-to-trust association, F (1, 239) = 11.348, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.045: the conflict effect was −0.811 in the black-box condition but −0.182 when a rationale was provided. The manipulation therefore concerns advice-judgment agreement rather than a direct experimental comparison of data-driven judgment with established experiential intuition. Because the scenarios did not establish objective recommendation accuracy, the moderation patterns are interpreted as changes in psychological response rather than as evidence that preserving trust or self-efficacy necessarily improves calibration, decision quality, or welfare.

items.title: When AI Enters the Pencil Box: A Longitudinal Study of Child–LLM Writing Collaboration in a Chinese Primary School
items.abstract: We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

items.title: When externally oriented motivation appears to matter: shared and unique associations with creative-process practices and learning engagement among Chinese art students
items.abstract: Introduction Motivation is closely related to students' engagement in learning, yet the associations of intrinsic motivation (IM) and externally oriented motivation (EM) may differ depending on whether they are examined separately or simultaneously. This study examined their shared and unique associations with self-reported creative-process practices (CPP) and learning engagement (LE) among Chinese university art students. Methods Survey data were collected from 481 students enrolled in art programs in one Chinese province using purposive sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to evaluate the four-factor measurement model, followed by structural equation modeling of three specifications: an IM-only model, an EM-only model, and a simultaneous IM-EM model. Results When examined separately, both IM and EM were positively associated with CPP and LE and showed significant indirect associations with LE through CPP. When modeled simultaneously, IM retained significant associations with CPP and LE, whereas the corresponding EM associations and its indirect association through CPP were smaller and no longer statistically significant. The CPP-LE association remained positive and statistically significant across all three model specifications. Discussion The findings indicate that externally oriented motivation can show meaningful associations when considered independently, but much of this association may overlap with intrinsic motivational variance. They also highlight the importance of distinguishing separate from unique motivational associations and of treating creative-process practices and learning engagement as related but conceptually distinct aspects of creative learning.

items.title: When is an LLM-as-a-Judge Good Enough?
items.abstract: Generative AI models are capable of generating human-like content, such as large language models (LLMs) generate texts. To automate processes, certain requirements regarding trustworthiness and correctness are fulfilled. To relieve people from controlling the created content, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge is available. In this scenario, another instance of an LLM is prompted to act as a judge, and check the generated content for certain quality requirements. However, such a judgement might not always align with a human judgement. Besides noise and errors in the human judgement, another reason is just the fact that different human evaluators can have different opinions about the evaluation. One reason could be that there might be no universal or unequivocal assessment since it is challenging to formulate objective rules. This natural existence of variance in human judgement defines the best possible benchmark level of alignment for a model judge. In this work, a method is presented to calculate this best possible benchmark under variance in human judgement. By comparing the distribution of the deviations between human judgement with the distribution of the deviation between model and human judgement with statistical means allows defining a model judge as good enough. Thus, a pragmatic way is provided to decide whether human judgement for a specific task can reliably be automated by a model judge in the quality that we can expect from the corresponding human judges. The code and prompts of the analysis performed are available under https://github.com/Ocean-code-1995/llm-judge-good-enough .

items.title: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI?
items.abstract: Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.

items.title: Why Bother Me Again? Benchmarking Personal Agent Memory for Interaction Preferences
items.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.

items.title: WSM-Aware HRI: An IoT-Enhanced Framework for Early Detection and Norm-Guided Repair of Failures with LLM Guidance
items.abstract: Human–robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world–state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human–robot interaction.

items.title: “Eyes on the Network” – Task Complexity and Expertise Shape Visual Strategies and Mental Workload in Rail Traffic Control
items.abstract: ObjectiveEvaluate the sensitivity of eye-tracking metrics to variations in mental workload in rail traffic control, and how they may be modulated by operator experience.BackgroundRail traffic control is a safety-critical domain characterized by high cognitive demands. While subjective workload measures are widely used, objective, real-time indicators, particularly eye-tracking metrics, remain underexplored.MethodEighteen professional rail traffic controllers (9 novice, 9 experienced) performed a simulation-based experiment involving four different scenarios with varying traffic density and task complexity, while wearing a head-mounted eye tracker. Measures of gaze behavior and visual strategies (fixations in different areas of interest (AOI)) were computed, and compared to subjective workload measures, to assess the effects of task difficulty and experience.ResultsSome measures like pupil dilation showed substantial changes (by ∼100%), while others like stationary gaze entropy showed more modest changes (∼40%), with increased task demand. Measures such as fixation rate revealed significant interaction effects with experience, indicating distinct visual strategies of novices vs. experts. Compared to experts, novices relied more on global overview displays under higher workload, and reduced planning-related information use, as revealed by AOI analysis. Subjective workload measures corroborated with increases in perceived demand.ConclusionThis study advances mental workload assessment in rail traffic control by demonstrating that eye-tracking metrics are sensitive to workload variations, and also reveal underlying cognitive strategies unique to expertise.ApplicationThese findings support the development of real-time workload monitoring systems and inform training interventions focused on information integration and cognitive strategies in rail traffic control operations.
