items.title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
items.abstract: The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

items.title: A Manifesto for the Age of Autonomous AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence moves beyond answering questions and begins acting on our behalf, institutions face two connected problems. People may retain formal authority while losing the practical conditions needed to exercise judgment. Meanwhile, AI systems can carry out technically correct actions without legitimate authorization. This manifesto argues for human agency, legitimate institutional authority, and accountable action. It examines meaningful human oversight, the limits of delegated authority, verification when actions produce consequences, and the obligations of those who govern AI. Its guiding principle, Authority Before Autonomy, calls for responsible delegation without surrendering the capacity to question, correct, and answer for what follows.

items.title: A Study on The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for Human Resource Management (HRM), including recruitment, employee selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, and workforce planning. This paper reviews the applications, potential benefits, challenges, and ethical considerations associated with AI in HRM. The study follows a descriptive approach based on secondary sources, including academic literature and professional reports. The review suggests that AI may support routine tasks, organize workforce information, and assist HR decisionmaking. However, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, accuracy, technical knowledge, and employee trust remain important concerns. The paper concludes that AI should support rather than replace human judgement, with responsible policies, data protection, and appropriate human supervision.

items.title: Academic integrity and artificial intelligence in initial teacher education: a documentary audit of teaching guides in Spanish universities
items.abstract: Purpose Universities are increasingly adopting institutional policies on academic integrity (AcI) and artificial intelligence (AI), but it remains unclear whether these expectations are translated coherently into the course-level documents that govern students’ learning and assessment. This article therefore examines how AcI and AI, including generative AI (GenAI), are articulated in official teaching guides for Spain’s Master’s Degree in Teacher Training, and whether guidance is embedded coherently across course design. Design/methodology/approach A documentary content analysis was conducted on 254 publicly available guides from 68 universities. Explicit AcI and AI references were coded across objectives, competencies, learning outcomes, activities and assessment. Two formative diagnostic indices measured breadth of coverage across these five sections. Mann–Whitney tests compared university and subject types; 25% of the corpus was independently double-coded. Findings AcI was mentioned in 53.5% of guides but was concentrated in assessment and competencies; 46.5% contained no valid reference. Explicit AI guidance remained marginal (6.3%) and primarily assessment-centred. Private universities showed slightly broader AcI coverage, public universities slightly broader AI coverage and Final Master’s Project guides substantially broader AcI coverage. Research limitations/implications The indices measure documentary breadth, not the quality, depth or implementation of guidance, and guides are nested within universities. Practical implications Programme leaders should integrate task-specific integrity and AI expectations across outcomes, activities, assessment, disclosure and formative support, with attention to future teachers’ professional AI literacy. Originality/value The study provides a large-scale, programme-specific audit and a transparent method for benchmarking cross-sectional curricular integration without treating document coverage as a quality score.

items.title: Advancing gender equity and inclusive digital futures through responsible agentic artificial intelligence governance
items.abstract: The shift to agentic AI represents a major paradigm change in the field of intelligent systems research and development, as these systems are capable of establishing sub-goals, planning for a goal, and executing plans with only minimal human oversight. This capability offers a unique chance to promote gender equality, inclusive digital engagement, and sustainable growth via evolving, accessible and fair AI-based methods throughout industries. Meanwhile, the increased autonomy of agentic AI systems presents unique challenges such as the potential for algorithmic bias to be amplified, decision-making disparities, and a lack of governance, each of which requires responsible AI, transparent governance, and clear ethical frameworks. This paper presents a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of a 41 paper corpus from Scopus. The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and summarizes the evidence regarding agentic and generative AI architectures, typologies of bias, and sectoral applications in healthcare, education, and gender equity. The paper presents a human-centred conceptual framework for responsible governance of agentic AI, building on lifecycle-governance and equity-by-design approaches, which merges bias mitigation, gender-inclusive design, and sustainability transition. The network of co-authorship is highly fragmented (density = 0.021; number of components = 37 from 88 authors), suggesting that there is no coordinated research agenda and giving empirical support to the integrative framework proposed here. This fragmentation further indicates that the vision and capabilities of agentic AI to contribute to gender equality and education are still not fully explored in the context of governance and sustainability, highlighting the relevance of the framework introduced in this paper. items.title: AI in Education from CAI to AGI: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping education, yet research remains fragmented across technological streams and often conflates technical capability with demonstrated educational effectiveness. This narrative review synthesizes representative literature published mainly between 2010 and 2026 to trace the evolution of AI-enabled education from computer-assisted instruction toward adaptive, immersive, generative, and potentially more general forms of intelligence. It compares three major technological streams: intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems, extended reality (XR), and large language model-based generative AI. The review finds that intelligent tutoring systems support learner modeling, adaptive feedback, and personalization, but their evidence base is methodologically heterogeneous. XR shows comparatively more consolidated evidence, particularly through systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with generally positive but context-dependent effects on engagement and learning outcomes. Generative AI expands dialogic explanation, scaffolding, content generation, and personalized support, although learner-outcome evidence remains limited relative to capability benchmarking. Building on these findings, the review proposes a Technology–Mechanism–Outcome–Challenge framework and argues that future progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) should be evaluated through learning mechanisms, measurable outcomes, human oversight, equity, and responsible governance.

items.abstract: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

items.title: AI-ASSISTED FINANCIAL JOURNALISM AND THE CREDIBILITY OF CORPORATE FINANCIAL INFORMATION IN NIGERIA
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI, natural language processing, machine learning and automated data-analysis systems, is transforming the production and dissemination of financial news. In Nigeria, where journalists increasingly rely on digital tools to interpret corporate disclosures, analyse financial statements and communicate market information to investors and the wider public, AI-assisted financial journalism presents both opportunities and credibility risks. This article examines the relationship between AI-assisted financial journalism and the credibility of corporate financial information in Nigeria. The study adopts an integrative literature-review approach, drawing on recent scholarly literature published between 2024 and 2026. The review is anchored on Source Credibility Theory, Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, Information Asymmetry Theory and Gatekeeping Theory. Seven recent empirical studies were critically reviewed, including studies of Nigerian journalists' AI adoption, newsroom practices, AI-attributed news credibility, AI disclosure and automated data-driven journalism. The review indicates that AI can improve the speed, analytical capacity, consistency and accessibility of financial journalism, particularly where journalists use AI to process large corporate datasets, identify anomalies, summarise reports and generate preliminary financial stories. However, the credibility benefits are not automatic. Risks arise from hallucinated information, inaccurate numerical interpretation, algorithmic bias, inadequate disclosure, overdependence on automated outputs, weak verification and the cultural and linguistic limitations of AI systems operating in Nigerian contexts. Recent Nigerian evidence also indicates that journalists are increasingly using AI for transcription, editing and preliminary drafting, while human journalists continue to retain important editorial responsibilities. The article argues that the credibility of AI-assisted financial journalism depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human verification, source transparency, professional competence, data provenance and institutional governance surrounding AI use. The article proposes a Human–AI Financial Journalism Credibility Framework in which AI performs computational and assistive functions while journalists retain responsibility for verification, interpretation, contextualisation and ethical publication. The study contributes to emerging literature by connecting AI-assisted journalism with the credibility of corporate financial information in an African emerging-market context.

items.title: AI-Driven Software Testing for a Test Center of Excellence: A Systematic Mapping and Evidence Synthesis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to automate and optimize software testing, but the evidence is distributed across heterogeneous testing activities, AI techniques, and evaluation measures. This study maps AI-driven software-testing research and translates the evidence into capabilities relevant to a Test Center of Excellence (TCoE). A systematic evidence workflow was applied to a unified audit corpus of 2,072 records, followed by focused eligibility reconciliation and full-text verification. The final focused evidence workset contains 29 records: 15 primary empirical studies, 9 secondary studies, 1 scope exclusion, and 4 full-text/access exclusions. The primary evidence covers machine learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary and search-based methods, deep learning, explainable AI, and large language models. The supported testing activities include test generation, selection and prioritization, minimization and optimization, fuzzing, validation, adaptive automation, and maintenance. The synthesis shows that AI should be treated in a TCoE as a governed capability layer rather than as a single automation tool. The proposed capability model links AI techniques to testing activities, measurable outcomes, reusable TCoE capabilities, and governance with human oversight. The study also identifies gaps in reliability, context awareness, test-oracle support, long-term maintenance, CI/CD integration, reproducibility, and standardized evaluation.

items.title: AI-Native Organizational Architecture (ANOA): A Unified Theory of Organizational Transition, Computational Production, Human Authority, Architectural Value Participation, and AI-Native Education
items.abstract: Abstract This working paper introduces AI-Native Organizational Architecture (ANOA), a theoretical framework for the structural transformation of enterprises and institutions operating in an increasingly autonomous computational economy. The research examines the limitations of conventional hierarchical organizations when artificial intelligence reduces information-processing and execution costs while introducing new challenges in coordination, institutional authority, accountability, and verification. ANOA proposes five interconnected organizational functions: Design, Human Authority, Orchestration, Execution, and Independent Assurance. Rather than establishing a rigid hierarchy, the framework separates architectural responsibility, legitimate decision authority, computational coordination, authorized execution, and independent verification. The paper develops mathematical hypotheses concerning computational productivity, architectural capital, organizational complementarities, coordination costs, and risk-adjusted economic value. It also introduces Architectural Value Participation (AVP), a proposed contractual mechanism linking compensation to independently attributable architectural contributions. The educational extension, ANOA-E, explores AI-native learning environments in which students interact directly with supervised large language models, formulate questions, critically evaluate explanations, and demonstrate independent reasoning. Philosophical judgment, practical wisdom, and accountable human authority are examined as complementary foundations for AI-native organizational governance. The study presents comparative organizational models, formal delegation mechanisms, falsifiable hypotheses, and a proposed empirical research agenda. ANOA is presented as a conceptual and testable framework rather than an empirically established organizational standard. Keywords: AI-Native Organizations; Organizational Architecture; Computational Economics; Human Authority; AI Governance; Architectural Capital; Organizational Productivity; Agentic AI; Verifiable Delegation; Architectural Value Participation; AI-Native Education; Critical Thinking. items.title: Alice and Bob, The Three Inevitabilities, and The Perfect AI Assistant
items.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a thought experiment in reverse alignment, in which, instead of aligning artificial intelligence (AI) with human values, we examine how humans inadvertently align with AI systems. We posit a theoretically perfect AI assistant and demonstrate that even this idealized system can produce concerning dynamics. In particular, we build on principles from pattern reinforcement and behavioral inertia to intuitively show that as the quality of AI assistance increases, human decision making tends to converge toward a utility-tilted sharpening of the assistant’s predictive distribution. Critically, this convergence exhibits strong path dependence: withdrawing assistance does not, by itself, restore cognitive independence, because the update contains no force that returns an agent to its pre-assistance policy. Recovery requires an active novelty incentive, and even then, it proceeds through history-dependent transients whose duration can exceed institutional planning horizons. We formalize these dynamics through two lenses: the Alice-Bob divergence , which tracks how adoption timing alone creates persistent cognitive divergence between identical agents, and the Three Inevitabilities , which captures the multi-scale forces (i.e. individual, social, and species-level) that drive convergence. Our theoretical and mathematical analysis reveals a fundamental trilemma: systems cannot simultaneously maintain optimal task outcomes, persistent human cognitive independence, and the absence of artificial novelty incentives. We conclude by identifying escape mechanisms and interventions that preserve human agency while retaining beneficial AI assistance to navigate the tension between augmentation and autonomy.

items.title: An Evidence-Grounded Framework for Evaluating AI-Generated Educational Feedback
items.abstract: Educational feedback generated by artificial intelligence is becoming more and more popular in teaching, but there are still differences in how to evaluate its quality in existing research. This study examined 68 empirical studies and compared the criteria, methods, evaluators, and evidence used in these evaluations. The results show that the relevant evaluation can be roughly summarised into three dimensions: Evidence Validity, Rubric and Task Alignment, and Pedagogical Usefulness. Evidence Validity focuses on whether the feedback is accurate and reliable, and is based on the learner's actual work. Rubric and Task Alignment focuses on whether the feedback meets the task requirements, evaluation criteria, and learner responses. Pedagogical Usefulness focuses on whether the feedback is clear, specific, actionable, and can support revision and further learning. The reviewed studies also used a variety of evidence to judge the quality of feedback, including human judgement, learner perceptions, revision behaviour, learning outcomes, and automated metrics. Based on these findings, this study proposes an evaluation framework that links different dimensions of feedback quality with corresponding evidence to provide clearer evaluation ideas for subsequent research and educational practice.

items.title: Artificial Emotional Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Emotional Intelligence (AEI) refers to Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that mediate human affect by sensing, processing, and responding to emotional states through multimodal inputs, including text, voice, and physiological signals (Chen et al. 2024 ). As AI systems (especially generative AI) become more conversational, personalised, and multimodal, AEI increasingly mediates therapy, companionship, customer service, education, and work (De Freitas et al. 2026 ; Zao-Sanders 2026 ). This marks a shift from mediating information and behaviour to mediating affect in sensitive contexts: AEI already underpins chatbots designed to mitigate suicide risk (Maples et al. 2024 ), customer-service systems that respond to frustration (Fan et al. 2024 ), and personalised sexbot applications (Rubinsztein and Ciriello 2024 ). This shift reflects technical progress, but also intensifies concerns about social fragmentation, care-capacity gaps, and the expansion of monetisation-oriented platform logics into domains historically organised around care, trust, and professional duty (Arsel 2026 ; Leong et al. 2021 ; Seleznova et al. 2023 ). Despite its significance, this reconfiguration of digital intermediation remains under-conceptualised in Information Systems (IS) research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Job Design: A Dynamic Framework
items.abstract: This study aims to deepen the understanding of artificial intelligence's (AI) impact on work by introducing and describing the AI-Job Dynamics Framework. Drawing from sociotechnical systems theory, complexity theory, and organizational learning theories, we conceptualize AI integration as a dynamic, non-linear process with three key phases. The framework, supported by theoretical propositions, identifies how this process affects organizational decision-making structures and key job characteristics over time, emphasizing the balance between centralization and decentralization of decision-making power. AI integration initially reduces job autonomy but may lead to greater autonomy in later phases as AI becomes more embedded. Throughout this process, AI reshapes skill requirements from routine to complex cognitive and adaptive skills. In the advanced phase of AI integration, we introduce the alternative paths and varied trajectories through which AI, organizational structures, and individual work experiences evolve. We conclude by discussing the implications of this framework for future research on AI and job design.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Predictive Analytics in Employee Retention: A Decision Support Approach
items.abstract: Employee retention has become a strategic concern for commercial enterprises because avoidable turnover can increase recruitment costs, disrupt organizational knowledge, and weaken workforce continuity. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework linking artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource practices, predictive analytics capability, employee data quality, AI-supported career development, organizational support for AI, employee engagement, and employee retention. The framework follows a quantitative survey design and combines descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, multiple regression, mediation analysis, PLS-SEM-oriented measurement assessment, and machine-learning validation. A dataset of 250 responses is used only to demonstrate the structure and presentation of statistical analysis; it is not claimed to represent actual field observations. The results indicate acceptable internal consistency, positive associations among the principal constructs, significant predictive relationships, and stronger predictive performance for nonlinear machine-learning models than the regression baseline. The study positions AI and predictive analytics not as replacements for managerial judgement but as decisionsupport mechanisms for identifying retention risks, targeting interventions, and improving evidence-based workforce planning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Research: A Critical Review of Current Developments, Challenges and Future Directions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been at the forefront of technological developments influencing business research. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled researchers to process increasingly complex data, automate analytical tasks and generate deeper insights. This study conducts a critical review of the evolution, applications, opportunities and challenges of AI in business research. Drawing upon contemporary literature from management, marketing, strategy, innovation, operations, finance and human resource management, the review synthesises knowledge regarding AI-driven decision-making, predictive analytics and knowledge creation. The review finds that AI improves research efficiency and supports evidence-based managerial decision-making. However, the literature highlights significant concerns relating to algorithmic bias, explainability, transparency, privacy, governance and research integrity. Existing scholarship is fragmented across disciplines and provides limited empirical evidence regarding the long-term implications of generative AI for research quality, organisational learning, governance effectiveness and human-AI collaboration. The study argues that AI should be viewed as a complementary capability that augments rather than replaces human expertise. By integrating evidence across multiple business functions, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps and develops a future research agenda focused on responsible governance, explainable AI and sustainable human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Evolving Roles of Teachers and Students in Human–AI Learning Ecosystems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force that is reshaping educational systems, pedagogical approaches, and learning environments. Similar to the impact of the Industrial Revolution on the development of mass education, the AI revolution has led to a fundamental reconsideration of educational objectives, teaching methods, curriculum structures, and the roles of teachers and students. Traditional educational models were largely teacher-centered and based on standardized curricula in which students acted as passive recipients of knowledge. In contrast, contemporary knowledge societies emphasize critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, problem-solving, and lifelong learning skills. In this context, AI technologies have accelerated the transition toward more learner-centered and personalized educational models. Subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, and big data analytics have increasingly entered educational environments through intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment tools, virtual assistants, and adaptive learning platforms. Applications such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Khan Academy’s Khanmigo illustrate the growing role of AI in teaching and learning processes. While these technologies provide significant opportunities for personalization, accessibility, and learning efficiency, they also raise ethical and social concerns related to data privacy, digital inequality, and academic integrity. This article systematically examines the historical and theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence in education and analyzes the evolving roles of teachers and students within AI-supported learning environments. Furthermore, the study evaluates the opportunities and challenges associated with AI integration and presents policy-oriented and practical recommendations for the ethical and effective implementation of AI technologies in education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration in Nursing Education: Perceived Barriers Among South African Nurse Educators and Nursing Students
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study investigates the perceived barriers to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into nursing education among nurse educators and nursing students at a public higher education institution in Gauteng, South Africa. Methods: A qualitative, exploratory, descriptive, contextual design was employed. Purposive sampling was used to recruit 12 nurse educators and 28 third-year nursing students. Data collection was conducted through semi-structured interviews with nurse educators and focus group discussions with nursing students. The data were analysed thematically, utilising Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework, with the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology(UTAUT) serving as an interpretative lens. Results: Four interrelated barriers emerged: infrastructure and resource constraints; limited AI literacy and skills; resistance and readiness challenges; and governance, ethical, and regulatory concerns. These barriers collectively influenced participants' willingness and capacity to engage with AI in nursing education. Conclusions: The effective integration of AI into nursing education necessitates coordinated institutional responses that address infrastructure, AI literacy, organisational readiness, and ethical governance. Developing contextually relevant policies, ensuring equitable access to technology, providing continuous professional development, and offering appropriate technical support may foster a more conducive environment for the responsible and sustainable integration of AI into nursing education.
